towns:Saint-Tropez.name: Saint-Tropez
towns:Saint-Tropez.teaser: Under the yachts, a fortified fishing port that still sells its catch on marble every morning
towns:Saint-Tropez.story: Strip away August and Saint-Tropez is a small fortified port on the south shore of its own gulf, named for Torpes, the martyr whose headless body, legend says, drifted ashore here in a boat. Every May since 1558 the Bravade carries his gilded bust through the streets to drums and musket fire. In the mornings fishermen lay out bream, red mullet and octopus on marble at the fish market behind the quay; on Tuesdays and Saturdays the plane trees of the Place des Lices shade the market, and by afternoon the gravel is a pétanque court again. By mid-October the town is its residents' again.
towns:Saint-Tropez.why: Come on a Saturday morning in autumn: the market under the planes, fish on the slabs, and room to walk the quay.
facts: Go for
The old port and its fish market at the Place aux Herbes, the lanes of La Ponche, the Place des Lices market (Tuesday and Saturday, 8am-1pm, all year; Oct 2026) and the boules in the afternoon
Best hour
Morning, before 10am; any month but August. The Bravade (16-18 May) and Les Voiles (late September) fill the town
Don't miss
The Citadelle, Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, the Musée de l'Annonciade and Sénéquier (all their own cards); the Musée de la Gendarmerie et du Cinéma in the old gendarmerie
Eat
La Ponche in the old fishing quarter, Colette at the Hôtel Sezz, La Vague d'Or at Cheval Blanc (all in the tables). Most hotel tables here close for winter from mid-October: check the season

sources.label: Saint-Tropez Tourisme — Le marché de Saint-Tropez

towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.name: Ramatuelle & Gassin
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.teaser: Two hill villages above Pampelonne, and an actor's plain grave under a laurel
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.story: Pampelonne's sand belongs to Ramatuelle, but the village turns its back on the beach clubs: an old village perched above the vines, its lanes wound in rings round the hill. Gérard Philipe, the actor of Le Cid, spent his holidays at his in-laws' house here and is buried in the village cemetery, near the school that carries his name. The grave, covered in ivy and shaded by a laurel, was kept deliberately one of the plainest there; a regional guide says he was buried in his Cid costume. On the next ridge Gassin is the other perched village, its terrace looking out over the whole gulf of Saint-Tropez.
towns:Ramatuelle & Gassin.why: Stand at Philipe's grave in Ramatuelle, then drive up to Gassin for the gulf at the end of the day.
facts: Go for
Two perched villages above the Pampelonne vineyards, and the long view over the gulf from Gassin
Best hour
Late afternoon, once the beach traffic has gone; Ramatuelle's open-air festival fills the village in early August
Don't miss
Gérard Philipe's grave in Ramatuelle's village cemetery; Gassin's terrace; the Belrose terrace at Gassin and the public end of Pampelonne (their own cards)
Eat
La Voile at La Réserve Ramatuelle and Club 55 on Pampelonne (both in the tables; seasonal, check before you go)

sources.label: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourisme — Gérard Philipe, Ramatuelle

towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.name: Bormes-les-Mimosas
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.teaser: A medieval village of stairs and covered passages that renamed itself for a flower in 1968
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.story: Until 1968 it was plain Bormes; that year the commune added '-les-Mimosas', for the yellow that covers its hills from January to March (where the tree came from is its own card's story). Every February since 1920 a corso fleuri has carried the flower through the streets, first on carts drawn by donkeys, then on tractors, now on floats dressed with some 12 tonnes of mimosa, with a battle of flowers on the Sunday. The rest of the year the old village is stairways and covered medieval passages such as the Ruelle des Sarrazins, climbing above the coast road, with Fort de Brégançon on its rock offshore.
towns:Bormes-les-Mimosas.why: Lose an hour in the stairways of the old village, then eat in a covered medieval lane.
facts: Go for
The stepped lanes and covered passages of the old village, and the view down to the coast
Best hour
Morning in the lanes; February for the mimosa and the corso (14-15 Feb in 2026, paid entry; book the Sunday)
Don't miss
The passages around the Ruelle des Sarrazins; Fort de Brégançon, booked through the Bormes tourist office (its own card)
Eat
Lou Portaou, on the Ruelle des Sarrazins (in the tables)

sources.label: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourisme — Le corso fleuri de Bormes-les-Mimosas

towns:Toulon.name: Toulon
towns:Toulon.teaser: The Var's capital is a navy port that feeds you honestly, for a third of a Saint-Tropez bill
towns:Toulon.story: Toulon is the Var's capital and a warship town, not a resort: grey hulls in the Rade, sailors on the quays, and tables that cost about a third of what the gulf charges. Walk up from the port into the Basse Ville, the old town, on a market morning and the air smells of chickpea batter: the cade, Toulon's own galette, is baked thin in wide copper pans and sold by the slice from carts along the Cours Lafayette. The town claims a second dish as its own, the sugared fried chichi frégi from the seafront kiosks. Mont Faron rises behind it all (its own walk card).
towns:Toulon.why: Give Toulon a market morning: cade from the cart, a natural wine at noon, and the Rade in front of you.
facts: Go for
The Rade and its warships, the old town, Toulon's own street food and the Var's natural-wine counters
Best hour
Morning, while the Cours Lafayette market runs (Tuesday to Sunday; closed Mondays)
Don't miss
The Cours Lafayette market (its own card); Superbuvette, Les Quilles and La Dégust' Nature for natural wine; the navy, in the curiosity 'Most of the French fleet sleeps in Toulon'
Eat
Shanaël near the Opéra, La Cade à Dédé's carts at Cours Lafayette and Le Mourillon (both in the tables)

towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.name: Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.teaser: Painted pointus on the quay, rosé at six, and a ten-minute boat to an island
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.story: Sanary still works for a living: the pointus, the painted wooden fishing boats of Provence, rock at their moorings along the quay, and the late-afternoon ritual is a cold rosé or a Bandol on a café table by the water, a saucer of tapenade and olives, pastis for the older men and the click of boules on the gravel. Just west along the coast, Le Brusc is the fishing harbour of Six-Fours-les-Plages, not of Sanary. From its Quai Saint-Pierre a boat crosses in about ten to twelve minutes to the Île des Embiez, where Paul Ricard, the pastis maker, lies on the island's highest point.
towns:Sanary-sur-Mer & Le Brusc.why: Take the quayside apéritif in Sanary at six, and the Embiez boat from Le Brusc the next morning.
facts: Go for
The pointus in the port, the apéritif on the quay, the boat from Le Brusc to the Embiez
Best hour
Wednesday morning for the market; early evening on the quay
Don't miss

The Wednesday market and the German exiles of the 1930s (their own cards); the Embiez boat from Le Brusc, all year, about hourly outside summer, adult €19 (Oct 2026, regional tourism listing; check iledesembiez.com)
Eat
Sanary's Wednesday market, cade included (its own card)

sources.label: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourisme — Navette maritime Le Brusc / Les Embiez
Figaro Nautisme — Île des Embiez au printemps (May 2026)

towns:Bandol.name: Bandol
towns:Bandol.teaser: The harbour that shipped Roman wine and lent its name to the Var's greatest red
towns:Bandol.story: Bandol is a harbour town before it is a label. The Romans terraced the slopes behind it and shipped their wine from this port, and the town gave its name to the appellation that now spreads over eight communes, some 70 estates and three cooperatives in the hills behind. Down here is where you taste them side by side, at the appellation's own Maison des Vins. On the first weekend of December the growers come down to the port for the Fête des Vins de Bandol, the new-vintage tasting that makes the coast's warmest winter day out. Offshore sits the small island of Bendor.
towns:Bandol.why: Time it for the December Fête des Vins, when the growers bring the new vintage down to the port.
facts: Go for
The port, a side-by-side tasting of the appellation, the island of Bendor
Best hour
Late morning, tasting before lunch; the first weekend of December for the Fête des Vins
Don't miss

The Maison des Vins de Bandol (its own card); the Fête des Vins de Bandol on the port, 5-6 Dec 2026 (old guide and one festival listing, Oct 2026; check before you go); the Bandol wine-country trip into the hills (its own card)
Eat
La Table du Castellet in the hills above the town; for the cellars, Château de Pibarnon at La Cadière-d'Azur and Domaine de Terrebrune at Ollioules (all in the tables)

sources.label: Festival en France — Fête des Vins de Bandol

towns:Hyères.name: Hyères
towns:Hyères.teaser: The Riviera's first winter town, all palms, villas and a medieval hill, before the islands
towns:Hyères.story: Hyères was taking winter visitors before most of the coast knew it had a season: it is often called the oldest winter resort of the Côte d'Azur, and the town's own heritage panels describe a 'ville à l'heure anglaise', an English winter town. Queen Victoria came in 1892 (the sources disagree on how long she stayed). The wealthy winterers built villas with acclimatisation gardens and planted the palms that line the boulevards. Behind them the medieval old town climbs its hill in steep lanes, and on Saturday mornings the Grand Marché des Îles d'Or spills along Avenue Gambetta and the Place Clemenceau.
towns:Hyères.why: Do the Saturday market, then climb the medieval lanes of the old town above the palms.
facts: Go for
The medieval old town, the palm boulevards and Belle Époque villas, the Saturday market
Best hour
Saturday morning, from about 7am, for the market; winter, the season the town was built for
Don't miss
Villa Noailles above the old town, the Giens peninsula and the islands (their own cards); Le Jardin du Café, the roaster on Rue Massillon (its own card)
Eat
La Colombe at La Bayorre, on the Toulon road (in the tables); bottles from Cave de la Capte (its own card)

sources.label: European Gardens — Var inventory, Plantier de Costebelle

towns:Collobrières.name: Collobrières
towns:Collobrières.teaser: The Maures village that calls itself chestnut capital, and proves it three Sundays every October
towns:Collobrières.story: Collobrières sits on its river deep in the Massif des Maures, a stone village ringed by chestnut groves that calls itself the capital of the chestnut. In October it proves it: the Fêtes de la Châtaigne fill three Sundays, in 2026 the 11th (Var producers' day), the 18th (the international day, when twin towns, brotherhoods and Italian flag-throwers parade) and the 25th (old trades and crafts). The rest of the year it is a quiet place of plane trees and an old bridge over the river, with the confectioner's shop facing it. For the record, a marron is a selected large-fruited chestnut, not a separate nut.
towns:Collobrières.why: Go on one of the October Sundays, early, and walk it off on a Maures trail afterwards.
facts: Go for
Chestnut country, the old bridge, the start of the best Maures walks (up to La Verne, up to Notre-Dame-des-Anges)
Best hour
An October Sunday before 9am: 18 and 25 Oct 2026 are still to come, 9am-6pm, free entry (Oct 2026, Le Lavandou and regional tourism listings); leave by 3pm
Don't miss
The festival shuttles from the Parking Ouest (in 2025: parking €2, shuttles free; check for 2026); the walk up to the Chartreuse de la Verne (its own card)
Eat
La Petite Fontaine on the Place de la République; marrons glacés at the Confiserie Azuréenne facing the Pont Vieux (both in the tables)

sources.label: Office de tourisme du Lavandou — Fêtes de la châtaigne et du terroir 2026
Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourisme — Chestnut and local produce festival, Collobrières

curiosities:The fig with its own appella.name: The fig with its own appellation
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.teaser: France grows one fig with an appellation, and nobody agrees how much of the country's crop it is
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.story: France has exactly one fig with its own appellation: the Figue de Solliès, the near-black Bourjassotte Noire of the Gapeau valley northeast of Toulon. It became an AOC in 2006 and a European AOP in 2011. It is picked from about 15 August into October and sold dead-ripe from the orchards and village stalls of the valley. What it weighs in the national harvest is a number everyone quotes and nobody quite agrees on.
curiosities:The fig with its own appella.why: Eat one in the valley in its last weeks; the larder card tells you where to buy.
facts: Touch it today
Mid-October is the tail of the harvest: the last AOP figs are on the stalls around Solliès-Pont (where to buy is the card 'The Solliès fig growers')
Where the sources argue

The Ministry of Agriculture says the appellation is 80% of France's fig production; other sources give about three-quarters; a 2025 trade report puts the Solliès basin at two-thirds to three-quarters; the cooperative alone is put at about 60%. The old guide said both 'three-quarters' and 'well over half'

sources.label: Ministère de l'Agriculture — Figue de Solliès

curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.name: The cork oak and the fire
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.teaser: A tree that loses its leaves to a forest fire and puts out green shoots a few weeks later
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.story: Drive into the Maures and the rock changes under the wheels: this massif is old crystalline schist, not the limestone of the rest of Provence, and its non-limestone soils grow chestnut and cork oak. The cork oak is built for fire. Its thick bark insulates the trunk, so when a blaze runs through, the tree loses its leaves and most of its small branches but the trunk is only scorched; within weeks green shoots break from the blackened limbs. The same bark, stripped from living trees, was the Maures' industry for centuries and corked the bottles of the south.
curiosities:The cork oak that survives t.why: Look at the trunks along the Maures roads: blackened bark with green growth on top is the whole story.
facts: Touch it today
The cork-oak woods around Collobrières and Gonfaron, where the massif's cork trade was based; the Maures burned badly in 2021, and the regrowth is visible from the roads
Where the sources argue

The State environment office (DREAL PACA) says cork-oak forests recover well only if fires are not too frequent, and abandoned, uncleared stands burn readily: 'survives the fire' holds for one fire, not for repeated ones

sources.label: RCF — climate change and the Massif des Maures

curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.name: The mimosa is Australian
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.teaser: The yellow that defines a Var winter came over the garden walls from Australia
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.story: The mimosa that turns the Maures yellow every winter is not from Provence at all. Acacia dealbata is Australian: it arrived on the Riviera as a garden plant in the 1800s, escaped over the walls and spread across the hills, until the coast came to think of it as its own. Bormes made the adoption official in 1968, when the commune renamed itself Bormes-les-Mimosas. Its corso began in 1920, with the flowers heaped on carts drawn by donkeys; tractors and then floats took over, and the 2026 parade was billed as the 83rd.
curiosities:The mimosa is Australian.why: Come in February and the import is the most local-looking thing in the Var.
facts: Touch it today
Nothing in flower in October: the trees bloom from January to March, and the corso is in mid-February in Bormes (14-15 Feb in 2026)
Where the sources argue

The 1920 start is Bormes's own date; a Var tourism page dates Provençal flower corsos generally to the late 19th century, and the old guide's 'oldest flower parade on the Côte d'Azur' was not confirmed

sources.label: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur Tourisme — Le corso fleuri de Bormes-les-Mimosas

curiosities:Why the islands are golden.name: Why the islands are golden
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.teaser: No treasure: the Îles d'Or are said to take their name from mica flashing in the rock
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.story: The Greeks called them the Stoechades, the islands 'in a row', one behind another: Porquerolles, Port-Cros and Le Levant strung along the horizon off Hyères. The golden name came later, usually dated to the Renaissance, and the usual explanation is the rock, not treasure: the islands are built of mica-schist, and under a low, slanting light the mica glints gold. Hyères keeps a folk tale as well, of a nobleman whose four daughters were famous for their beauty and for swimming off the coast. Neither version rests on a document the sources produce.
curiosities:Why the islands are golden.why: Watch the island shores from the boat late in the day and decide for yourself.
facts: Touch it today
From the boat to Porquerolles or Port-Cros in late-afternoon light, watch the schist of the shore cliffs (the islands trip card owns the ferry)
Where the sources argue
The Renaissance date and the mica-schist explanation are widely repeated (Routard, regional guides) but no primary source was found; the folk tale of the four daughters is the alternative

sources.label: Routard — Les îles d'Or, l'archipel nature de la Côte d'Azur

curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.name: Most of the French fleet sleeps in Toulon
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.teaser: Over 60% of the French navy's tonnage ties up in one Var roadstead
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.story: Toulon's fate was its roadstead, deep and sheltered. Henri IV founded a shipyard here in 1599; Richelieu and then Colbert enlarged it, and Vauban designed the new basin, the darse Vauban. Today the arsenal covers some 268 hectares behind about 10 km of quays: the largest naval base in the Mediterranean and in Western Europe, home port of the carrier Charles de Gaulle and of the navy's nuclear attack submarines, and the berth of more than 60% of the French fleet's tonnage. Its two largest drydocks are given as 422 m by 40 m; work on the 400 m docks began in 1911.
curiosities:Most of the French fleet sle.why: Take the boat round the Rade: the grey hulls are the most permanent thing on this coast.
facts: Touch it today
The arsenal is a military zone; see it from a boat tour of the Rade from Quai Cronstadt on the old port, or from Mont Faron above (its own card)
Where the sources argue
Tonnage share is usually given as over 60% (Assystem, GlobalMilitary), some older sources say 70%; the old guide's 20,000 staff was not re-checked

curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.name: The river the Var lost in 1860
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.teaser: The Var is named for a river that has not flowed through it since 1860
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.story: Until 1860 the river Var was a frontier: the department's eastern edge ran along it, with the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia on the far bank. When Nice was annexed that year, France rebuilt the Alpes-Maritimes from the county of Nice and, taken from the Var, the arrondissement of Grasse. The river ended up entirely outside the department, and the Var kept its name anyway, a department named for water that no longer touches it. The same line explains a sandwich: the pan bagnat sold on Var beaches is Niçois, from across a border barely a century and a half old.
curiosities:The river the Var lost in 18.why: Drop it at lunch over a pan bagnat: the department, and the sandwich, belong to two sides of an 1860 border.
facts: Touch it today
Order a pan bagnat on a Var beach and know it is an import: pan banhat, 'bathed bread', in the old Nissart tongue
Where the sources argue
One source calls a department not watered by its namesake river unique in France; that was not confirmed

curiosities:15 August 1944.name: 15 August 1944
curiosities:15 August 1944.teaser: Provence's own D-Day: the landing that freed Toulon and Marseille in under a fortnight
curiosities:15 August 1944.story: Normandy has its D-Day; Provence has 15 August 1944. At 8am Operation Dragoon put Allied troops ashore on beaches between Toulon and Cannes, the main landings strung from Cavalaire to Saint-Raphaël. Some 350,000 men were engaged, about 250,000 of them in General de Lattre de Tassigny's French Army B. The prize was the two great ports, which could then land men and supplies for the drive north: Marseille was freed on 28 August, and Toulon fell in the same last days of the month, under a fortnight after the landing. Provence remembers it as its own liberation.
curiosities:15 August 1944.why: Stand at the memorial on Mont Faron and look down at the port the landing was fought for.
facts: Touch it today

The Mémorial du Débarquement et de la Libération en Provence on the summit of Mont Faron (the cable car belongs to the Mont Faron walk card; check opening); the landing beaches of the Cavalaire bay are in the sister guide at /terroir/Cavalaire-sur-Mer/
Where the sources argue

Troop numbers: about 350,000 for the operation (Ministry of the Armed Forces), the French share given as 250,000 or 260,000 (Hérodote); the old guide's 'half a million' is not supported. The exact day of Toulon's liberation was not pinned in the sources checked

Chemins de mémoire — La route du débarquement de Provence

curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.name: Sanary, capital of German letters
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.teaser: In 1933 a Var fishing port became the capital of German literature in exile
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.story: After Hitler took power in 1933, a small fishing port in the Var filled with German-speaking writers. The critic Ludwig Marcuse called Sanary the 'capital of German literature in exile': Thomas Mann and his son Klaus, Lion Feuchtwanger, Franz Werfel and Alma Mahler, Stefan Zweig among those who came. Aldous Huxley was there before them: he bought a house in 1930, wrote Brave New World in it, and from 1933 welcomed the exiles. The war scattered the colony again. A plaque now lists 36 German-language writers and artists who lived here in those years.
curiosities:Sanary, capital of German le.why: Read the 36 names on the plaque, then look at the quiet port they chose to wait in.
facts: Touch it today
The plaque with the 36 names, in the patio of the Sanary tourist office (town heritage guide); the town's exile heritage panels
Where the sources argue

The colony's span is given as 1933-1940, 1933-1942 or, on the plaque, 1933-1945; the regional tourism site says Brecht finished The Threepenny Opera in Sanary, but other sources place that 1928 work at Le Lavandou, years before the exile
